stemBlocks.value: Dot plots show the test scores of 15 students from School X (52, 54, 57, 59, 61, 63, 65, 67, 69, 71, 73, 75, 77, 80, 82) and 15 students from School Y (43, 47, 50, 54, 58, 61, 64, 67, 70, 73, 76, 80, 84, 87, 91); the accompanying table gives standard deviations of 9.1 for School X and 14.3 for School Y. (a) Calculate the mean score for each school. (b) Determine the median score for each school. (c) Determine the lower quartile and upper quartile for School X. (d) Calculate the interquartile range for School X.
Think first: Read the 15 scores off each plot in order — with an odd number of values, position does all the work.

contentBlocks.value: With 15 values the median is the 8th, and that score is 67 in both plots

solutionSteps.instruction: Take the 4th and 12th scores for School X.

contentBlocks.value: Q1 is the (15 + 1) ÷ 4 = 4th value and Q3 is the 3(15 + 1) ÷ 4 = 12th value

strategyBlocks.value: Total each school's 15 scores and divide by 15 for the mean; take the 8th score as the median, and for School X take the 4th and 12th scores as the quartiles.

finalAnswerBlocks.value: (a) Mean = 67 for School X and 67 for School Y  (b) Median = 67 for each school  (c) For School X, Q1 = 59 and Q3 = 75  (d) IQR for School X = 16

whyThisWorks.value: The two schools share both a mean and a median, so central tendency alone cannot tell them apart — the whole difference lies in spread, which is why the standard deviations (9.1 against 14.3) matter. Quartiles cut ordered data into four equal-sized groups, so the interquartile range describes the middle half of the students and ignores the extremes at each end.
